title: Final: assemblies and versions
sub: Identity, binding, strong names and NuGet
cards/0/q: A .NET Framework 4.8 app. A signed library was built against Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.0.0, the folder has 13.0.0.0, and App.exe.config has no redirect. What happens?
cards/0/options/1: 13.0.0.0 loads: the version is no lower than requested
cards/0/options/2: Both versions load: each for its own consumers
cards/0/options/3: A warning in the Fusion log, and the app carries on
cards/0/explain: For a strong-named assembly Framework requires an exact version match. The "no lower" rule belongs to .NET Core and .NET 5+.
cards/0/wrong/1: That is how .NET 8 behaves, not Framework.
cards/1/q: Which of these change an assembly identity? Select all.
cards/1/explain: The identity is name, version, culture and public key. FileVersion and InformationalVersion are plain attributes; the CLR loader ignores them.
cards/2/q: A signed netstandard2.0 library. Which line should change so that 3.7.x patches do not require binding redirects for Framework consumers?
cards/2/explain: AssemblyVersion should be 3.0.0.0 — major only. Deleting the line is not enough: the SDK derives 3.7.2.0 from Version. Let the patch and CI build numbers live in Version and FileVersion.
cards/3/q: Acme.Pricing requires Acme.Log >= 2.1, Acme.Tax requires Acme.Log >= 2.0. The server has 2.0, 2.2 and 3.0, but no 2.1. What does NuGet pick?
cards/3/explain: It needs the lowest version that satisfies both: at least 2.1. There is no 2.1, and the next available one is 2.2.
cards/3/wrong/1: NuGet does not take the newest: the rule is the lowest applicable.
cards/4/q: Put in order how a .NET 8 app gets the Acme.Log assembly
cards/4/items/0: At build time the SDK writes App.deps.json from the restore result
cards/4/items/1: hostfxr reads runtimeconfig.json and picks the framework
cards/4/items/2: hostpolicy builds the TPA from the app and framework deps.json
cards/4/items/3: Code touches a type from Acme.Log for the first time
cards/4/items/4: The default context finds Acme.Log in the TPA by name and checks the version
cards/4/explain: First restore and build, then the host builds the assembly list, and only when the JIT meets a type from Acme.Log does the assembly load — by name from the list, with the "no lower" check.
cards/5/q: The Money class moved from Shop.dll to Shop.Core.dll. Make old programs find it
cards/5/explain: TypeForwardedTo writes a row into ExportedType, and the CLR follows it to Shop.Core. TypeForwardedFrom goes on the type itself in the new assembly — serializers read it, not the loader.
cards/6/q: Match the .NET Framework mechanism to what became of it in modern .NET
cards/6/pairs/0/1: Shared assemblies in the installed runtime folder
cards/6/pairs/1/1: Not needed: a version no lower than requested fits
cards/6/pairs/2/1: Lookup by name in the TPA list from deps.json
cards/7/q: A colleague says: "Let us strong-name the assembly, and nobody will be able to swap our code." Is he right?
cards/7/options/0: No: a strong name is identity, not protection; Authenticode and NuGet package signing prove the author
cards/7/options/1: Yes: the CLR checks the signature on every load
cards/7/options/2: Yes, but only in .NET 8 and later
cards/7/options/3: No: only Microsoft assemblies may be strong-named
cards/7/explain: The modern runtime does not check the strong-name signature, Framework has long skipped it during normal loading too, and the keys of many libraries are public.
cards/8/q: A .NET 8 app was built against Acme.Pricing with AssemblyVersion 3.7.0.0. Deployment put the old 3.6.0.0 assembly into the folder. What happens?
cards/8/options/0: FileLoadException: the version found is lower than requested
cards/8/options/1: It loads: only the major version is checked
cards/8/options/2: It loads: .NET 8 does not check versions
cards/8/explain: "No lower" cuts both ways: higher is fine, lower is a load error. MissingMethodException would happen if both had AssemblyVersion 3.0.0.0 and the check passed.
